intro: The accessibility rules that come up most in reviews and interviews.

entries.medium: The four WCAG principles, each with success criteria at levels A, AA and AAA. AA is the common target and what most legislation references.
entries.detail: Robust means semantic, valid markup, which is why using the right element is the most common fix across all four principles.

entries.short: Everything interactive is reachable and operable without a mouse.
entries.medium: Native elements bring keyboard support for free. Tab order follows the DOM, so avoid positive tabindex. Focus must be visible, styled with :focus-visible rather than removed.
entries.detail: Putting the mouse away and using the page is the fastest accessibility test there is.

entries.short: Move focus when content appears, restore it when it goes.
entries.medium: Opening a dialog moves focus into it and traps it until close, then returns focus to the trigger. Mark the rest of the page inert so it is not focusable or announced.
entries.detail: The native dialog element with showModal handles focus, trapping and the backdrop for you.

entries.short: Changes what is announced, never what the element does.
entries.medium: Use it only to fill a gap a native element cannot cover, such as naming an icon-only button or reporting state. Prefer a native element over adding a role to a div.
entries.detail: Bad or redundant ARIA is worse than none. role=button on a div still needs focus, key handlers and form behaviour.

entries.short: What assistive tech reads out for every control.
entries.medium: The accessible name comes from content, a label, aria-label or aria-labelledby. The role usually comes from the element. States such as aria-expanded and aria-checked must stay in sync with the UI.
entries.detail: Inspect the accessibility tree in DevTools to see exactly what is announced rather than guessing.

entries.short: Every control needs an accessible name.
entries.medium: Use a label with for=id or wrap the input. Groups of radios and checkboxes get a fieldset with a legend. Icon-only buttons get aria-label. Placeholders are not labels.
entries.detail: An unlabelled field is announced as just 'edit text', which gives the user no idea what to type.

entries.short: 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text and UI.
entries.medium: Large text is about 24px or 18.66px bold. Meaningful icons, input borders and focus indicators need 3:1 against their background. Disabled controls are exempt.
entries.detail: Muted gray text is the most common failure. Darkening it one step usually fixes it without hurting the design.

entries.short: Never use color as the only way to convey meaning.
entries.medium: Errors marked only in red, charts distinguished only by hue and links that differ only by color all fail. Add an icon, a pattern, a label or an underline.
entries.detail: This affects people with color vision deficiency and anyone in bright sunlight, which is a much larger group than it sounds.

entries.short: A logical outline and regions let users navigate quickly.
entries.medium: One h1 per page and no skipped levels for visual reasons. header, nav, main, aside and footer give a map. main appears once.
entries.detail: Screen reader users jump by heading and landmark far more than they read linearly.

entries.short: Describe the image, or mark it decorative.
entries.medium: Meaningful images need alt that conveys the same information as the image. Decorative images use alt="" so they are skipped. Avoid starting with 'image of'.
entries.detail: For complex images such as charts, the alt gives the takeaway and a longer description carries the detail.

entries.medium: Reduced motion means fewer and gentler animations, not zero: keep opacity and color, drop movement and parallax. Nothing should flash more than three times a second.
entries.detail: Auto-playing carousels should pause, and any moving content longer than five seconds needs a way to stop it.

entries.short: Automated tools catch a subset; people and keyboards catch the rest.
entries.medium: axe and Lighthouse find missing names and contrast issues but miss focus order, meaning and keyboard traps. Test with the keyboard, at 200% zoom, and with a real screen reader.
entries.detail: The accessibility tree in DevTools shows exactly what is exposed, which is faster than guessing from the DOM.
